label: The vertical-offset (+C) control's first payoff: in-04-02 'Pinning Down the Constant'. The authored reveal argues that sliding a curve up cannot tilt it, so f′ carries no information about vertical position — and until now no engine could let a learner DO that. derivativeTrace gained an offsetMax control (local state, never graded, because a grader that could see C would contradict the claim), and this insertion puts it where the argument is made.

step.body: The reveal made a claim about the whole family at once. Now hold the family in your hands: slide the curve and watch the derivative refuse to react.

predict.prompt: The top pane shows f(x) = x², the bottom traces f′. If you slide the WHOLE curve upward, what happens in the f′ pane?

options.label: f′ rises too — the curve went up
Nothing at all — f′ does not move
f′ tilts, because the curve is steeper up there

predict.reveal: Nothing moves. Sliding a curve up does not tilt it anywhere, so every member of the family x² + C has the identical derivative 2x. That is why the derivative alone can never tell you which member you have — and why an initial condition is not extra calculus, it is the missing information put back.

widget.prompt: Slide C until the curve passes through the point (1, 5), then bring x to 1. Watch the f′ pane the whole time.
widget.successFeedback: At x = 1 the tangent's slope is 2 — and it was 2 for every single value of C you slid through, because a vertical shift tilts nothing. The point (1, 5) is what picked C = 4 out of the infinite stack: 1 + C = 5. The derivative gave you the shape; one point gave you the position.
widget.lowFeedback: You are left of x = 1. Keep going — and notice that whatever you do with the C slider on the way, the f′ trace underneath is unchanged.
widget.highFeedback: You have gone past x = 1. Come back — and watch the f′ pane as you slide C: it does not care where the curve sits vertically, which is the whole reason C survives differentiation unseen.

refusals.title: Chains Within Chains (derivative-rules)
refusals.why: Represents gate. The reveal's subject is RULE ORDER — outermost operation first, inner rules afterwards, never two rules in one line — on x²·(3x+1)⁴. derivativeRuleLab's mode enum is product|chain (schema.ts DerivativeRuleLabSpec): it can demonstrate either rule alone, but the lesson's claim is about how they NEST, and a lab that runs one rule shows the ingredient while the lesson asks about the assembly order. Same failure shape as the dr-03-02 refusal in S205E. Needs a nested-rule engine that exposes the decomposition tree; recorded as an engine gap.

refusals.title: Changing the Limits (integration-accumulation)
refusals.why: Represents gate. The reveal contrasts two correct u-substitution routes and names the error of mixing them (integrate in u, evaluate at x-limits). riemannSum and accumulateArea both draw a single integrand over a single interval (schema.ts: fn enums line|square and const|line|square|shifted); neither represents a CHANGE OF VARIABLE, so the two worlds the lesson keeps apart cannot both appear, and the named error has nowhere to happen on screen. A lab showing one interval's area would demonstrate that limits matter — true, but not the lesson's claim. Needs a substitution engine showing x-world and u-world side by side; recorded as an engine gap.
